Music, mood & migraine

Personal comfort is a promising starting point.

Research supports studying music people find comforting. It does not establish a universal migraine-relieving frequency, or show that a spectrogram can identify one.

Why a sad song can feel good

Music can match how you feel while making the experience feel understood, meaningful or easier to process. A survey of 772 people associated enjoyment of sad music with emotion regulation, empathy, imagination and experiencing sadness without the consequences of a real-life loss. This is self-report evidence, not proof that sad music improves everyone's mood. [1]

What you want from music also changes with the situation: company, activity, attention and current arousal can affect your choice. A ten-day smartphone study found substantial variation within the same person. “What comforts you now?” is therefore a better question than assuming one permanent taste profile. [2]

Preferences concern combinations of pitch, timbre, rhythm, memory and learned expectations—not just isolated frequencies. Cross-cultural experiments found that the Tsimane’, with little exposure to Western music, did not share Western listeners’ preference for consonant over dissonant harmonies. Some apparently natural preferences are shaped by experience. [3]

Why binaural audio might help you

For example, a 200 Hz tone delivered to one ear and a 206 Hz tone to the other can produce a perceived 6 Hz beat. The audible carriers and their difference are different quantities. A binaural beat is not evidence that the whole brain has switched to a 6 Hz state. A review of 14 EEG studies found inconsistent entrainment results. [7]

Your reported relief is worth taking seriously; its mechanism remains uncertain. Relaxation, attention shifting away from pain, emotional engagement, a sense of control, expectations and the listening/rest routine are plausible contributors. Music preference and perceived choice have experimental support in pain studies, but those findings do not identify why a particular recording helps your migraine. [4] [5]

Comfort, pain relief and prevention of future migraine attacks are separate outcomes. The prototype explores comfort; it cannot establish treatment efficacy.

What the studies actually show

This is a focused evidence review, not an exhaustive systematic review.

Sad music
Taruffi & Koelsch, 2014 [1]		Online survey, 772 participants. Multiple emotional rewards and situational influences were reported.Retrospective, self-selected responses; associations do not establish causation or universal benefit.
Everyday context
Greb et al., 2019 [2]		119 frequent music listeners; 14 prompts/day for 10 days. Situation and the purpose of listening predicted music selection.Observational, mostly young adults; perceived music characteristics rather than automatically measured acoustics.

What frequency analysis can—and cannot—do

A Fourier transform describes frequency content; a spectrogram tracks how it changes over time. These can describe brightness, tonal peaks, noise-like texture and temporal variation. They do not measure a listener's emotion, brainwaves, pain or clinical response.

For a possible binaural pair, retain and inspect left and right channels separately: mono mixing loses the ear-specific presentation. A spectral peak near 200 Hz is an audible component, not a 200 Hz brain rhythm. Complex music can contain many unrelated peaks, so subtracting two peaks is not reliable proof of an intended binaural beat.

Humming mainly preserves a melody or pitch contour. It does not recreate the original recording's texture, production, spectrum or stereo beat. Song identification, melody retrieval and similarity recommendation are separate engineering problems.

Sound features + personal feedback + current context → candidate comfort

Product hypothesis: matching a person's preferences and learning from their feedback may produce more comfortable choices than a generic “migraine frequency” playlist. That is a hypothesis to test, not a clinical claim. Audio similarity is a way to generate candidates; the person's response is the outcome.

From this prototype to a music product

The working demo uses signal processing and procedural synthesis. Its three sound recipes are tuned using the reference’s spectral peak and brightness; a simple rule then reorders them using your comfort ratings in the same mood and surroundings. It is not a trained AI model or a catalog search, and its rankings are not calibrated predictions.

  1. Recognize the input. For a playing recording, use fingerprints against an authorized music catalog. For humming, use a melody embedding that tolerates key and tempo differences. These are different tasks: see Wang’s Shazam paper and Google’s Hum to Search research.
  2. Retrieve candidates. Combine acoustic descriptors and audio embeddings with tags such as timbre, vocals, tempo, familiarity and the person’s current preferences. Evaluate on held-out listening sessions; similarity alone is not evidence of comfort.
  3. Generate variations. A later licensed music-generation model could propose new textures or arrangements. Keep provenance and usage rights clear. Check abrupt transients, excessive level changes and stereo output; give users control before playback.
  4. Learn cautiously. Collect explicit consent for any future server-side audio or health-data processing. Start with personal comfort ratings and dislikes, and compare recommendation quality against simple baselines before introducing medical claims.

Why Still builds a personal comfort profile

The comfort profile rests on one finding that recurs across this evidence: people differ, and the same person differs across a migraine cycle. These sources were checked against the original papers in November 2026. Strength describes the evidence, not the app.

FindingEvidenceWhat Still does with it
Sound becomes aversive at lower levels in migraine, and lower again during attacksAshkenazi et al., 2009 (60 migraine, 52 controls): aversion thresholds of 90.4 dB vs 105.9 dB between attacks, and 76.0 dB during attacks. Group means for pure tones in a calibrated lab. Moderate. SourceFour states (normal, warning signs, during an attack, recovering) with cautious offsets of 0, −6, −14 and −6 dB. These are starting points, not measurements of you.
The comfortable range is narrower across most frequenciesMourgela et al., 2023 (55 migraine, 49 controls, online, uncalibrated): narrower range at 12 of 13 tones from 100 Hz to 12 kHz. Moderate. SourceA seven-band comfort contour. Bands you mark lower are turned down, never boosted, by at most 12 dB.

How you ask changes the answerIkumi et al., 2022 (35 high-frequency/chronic migraine, 25 controls): rising-level methods gave lower thresholds than randomised levels, which the authors attribute to avoidance. Listeners disagree about the same soundEmoSynth (168 synthetic sounds, 40 annotators): the average standard deviation of pleasantness ratings was 1.2 on a 1–5 scale, and 1 or more for 90% of sounds (our analysis of public labels). Slow, regular modulation is gentler than fast flutterVirjonen et al., 2019: periodic amplitude modulation of broadband sound adds an annoyance penalty. Moderate. SourceThe only movement is one slow rise and fall every 6–12 seconds, starting at about 1 dB and capped at 1 dB during attacks.

Mantiuk et al., 2012 found forced-choice comparisons gave the lowest measurement variance. Moderate. Nielsen · Mantiuk“Which felt calmer?” A/B rounds with a preference model (Chu & Ghahramani, 2005). In our simulations of listeners with different hidden favourites, 16 choices cut the distance to their favourite from 0.58 to 0.27, against 0.36 for random choices.

SourceNo “pain reduced by X” badges. Comfort is the outcome. Any pain comparison needs a planned, within-person design.
Wellness wordingFDA General Wellness guidance (January 2026) gives relaxation coaching that “may help” people live well with migraine as an example of an acceptable wellness claim. Strong. SourceStill describes comfort and self-knowledge. An automated test fails the build on treatment claims.

The full verified strategy, including what the evidence does not support, is in the repository at docs/product-strategy.md.

A useful next experiment

Begin with usability and tolerability. The primary POC endpoint should be reported comfort, with pain change recorded as exploratory. The current prototype is a demonstration and feedback tool; it does not implement the randomized study described below.

  1. Repeat comparisons within each consenting person. Compare their preferred audio with an added beat, an otherwise closely matched version without the beat, and quiet rest. Match the two audio versions in duration and perceived level. Allow silence as a valid preference.
  2. Randomize order across suitable sessions. Use neutral labels for the audio versions, conceal the beat assignment where feasible, and avoid implying either is therapeutic. Quiet rest cannot be fully blinded. Plan separation between sessions to reduce carryover.
  3. Record before and after. Capture comfort, pain (0–10), sound sensitivity, mood, time and migraine phase, environment, headphones, volume setting, listening duration, sleep and medication/timing. Device volume is not a calibrated ear-level dB measurement.
  4. Keep usual care available. Do not delay or withhold migraine treatment. Stop audio if it worsens symptoms. Record early stops and worsening alongside improvements; never label these sessions as successful engagement.
  5. Evaluate the actual question. Predefine comfort improvement and tolerability measures. Compare repeated within-person outcomes, quantify uncertainty and include all assigned sessions. Medication, natural attack resolution, expectations and missing data can affect results. A clinical efficacy study needs a clinician/research partner, suitable ethics review and a prespecified protocol.

How to use the YouTube feedback

Follow-up: we retrieved 30-second excerpts from all three recordings and reviewed 100 top plus 100 recent comments per video (557 distinct comment IDs). See the measured spectra, sampling details and qualitative findings. These measurements and comments do not establish a treatment effect.

Comments can suggest interview questions and candidate sounds. They are not efficacy labels: commenters are self-selected, diagnoses and concurrent treatments are unknown, unsuccessful experiences may be missing, and improvement can coincide with natural symptom changes. Use consented, structured feedback for learning, and keep perceived comfort separate from migraine treatment outcomes.
